entry.heading: Attack on Titan (Shingeki no Kyojin)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived freely and for the people you love, but freedom pursued through violence spreads the hatred it means to escape; the story asks the reader to keep looking for understanding even when the world is cruel.

frames.aligns: Evil is shown to bring understanding, not made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7); self-sacrifice for friends; the dignity of the enemy shown from inside Marley; forgiveness (the Blouse family toward Gabi).
frames.concerns: A "devil" origin myth; no hope beyond death; a suicide attempt (CCC 2280-2283).

frames.aligns: Repentance as a long road (Reiner, Gabi); the burden of killing even in war.
frames.concerns: "Devil" pact imagery may be a concern where evil spirits are taken as real; no transcendent hope. Guarding the senses (nepsis) makes the gore itself a serious concern.

frames.aligns: Clear picture of sin passed down and of human evil; sacrifice for others; revenge shown to destroy. Views vary by congregation, since each church is self-governing.
frames.concerns: "Devil" pact as myth; no gospel answer.

frames.aligns: Christian writers draw out sin, sacrifice and overcoming evil with good (Thirst.sg and Christ and Pop Culture titles; not opened). Depicts a mass killer without endorsing him.
frames.concerns: Nihilistic voices (Kenny, Zeke); a hero who becomes a mass killer needs careful reading.

frames.aligns: Longing for freedom and deliverance; forgiveness.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": power from a pact with a "devil" (ch. 122); Paths and a spirit world binding a people.

frames.aligns: Realism about total depravity: no one is innocent, including the heroes. Common grace lets readers value the art and its questions.
frames.concerns: Little answer beyond human effort; a suicide attempt (WLC Q136).

frames.aligns: Two-kingdoms questions: governments lie and wage war, yet order matters. Law exposes guilt (Reiner, Gabi).
frames.concerns: Little gospel (forgiveness is human, not divine). LCMS and ELCA families may weigh the content differently.

frames.aligns: Prevenient grace glimpsed in former enemies changing (Gabi, Reiner); social holiness against ethnic hatred.
frames.concerns: Profanity; no transcendent hope. Holiness churches more cautious about the content than UMC.

frames.aligns: Just-war tradition (Article 37) fits the story's questions; forgiveness of enemies; works judged by how they frame good and evil.
frames.concerns: Suicide attempt; no transcendent hope. Episcopal and ACNA families may differ on the gender questions.

frames.aligns: Violence is not shown as heroic in the end: it is a cycle that corrupts everyone, and the ending sides with Armin's choice to talk rather than kill.
frames.concerns: Most conflicts are still settled by force; children trained as soldiers. Old Order and conservative groups avoid most popular media regardless; MC USA families may read it as an anti-war text.

frames.aligns: Courage, sacrifice and family love; repentance of former enemies.
frames.concerns: Eren's preemptive war; no afterlife hope; a suicide attempt.

frames.aligns: Death shown as final rather than as roaming spirits; the cost of hatred; forgiveness.
frames.concerns: The Paths and a "devil" origin myth. Glorified violence is a concern, though the story does not glorify it in the end.

frames.aligns: Christian neutrality echoed: war and nationalism are shown to destroy everyone; honesty about guilt.
frames.concerns: A "devil" pact myth; the military as the main path for the heroes.

frames.aligns: Understanding ends hatred; fear shown as the root of violence.
frames.concerns: Evil, fear and death shown as overwhelming realities; despair.

frames.aligns: Peace-and-justice reading: a critique of ethnonationalism, propaganda and dehumanization; anti-war ending.
frames.concerns: Critics' concern that Holocaust imagery is used carelessly (New Republic, JTA); a female lead centered on a man.

frames.aligns: Memory of persecution and the cost of dehumanization; respect for life.
frames.concerns: Armbands, internment zones and a "euthanasia" plan echo the Holocaust (ch. 86-88, 114); some see antisemitic tropes (Eldians as a "devil" people whose blood carries power). Many Haredi homes restrict such media altogether.

frames.aligns: Memory of persecution; self-defense debated; respect for life.
frames.concerns: Split on whether the Eldian story honors or distorts Holocaust memory (JTA); Jewish dignity is a stated family concern.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam: critique of ethnonationalism and dehumanization.
frames.concerns: Attention to antisemitism and stereotypes: some Jewish fans quoted by JTA felt the Holocaust reduced to a "trope," while Israeli scholars in the same piece read it as about Japanese militarism.

frames.aligns: Justice for the oppressed; courage; the horror of killing innocents is not hidden; collective guilt rejected.
frames.concerns: A "devil" pact as source of power; spiked wine; a suicide attempt (forbidden). Titan nudity is non-sexual.

frames.aligns: Dharma and righteous war are central questions; karma-like cycles of action and consequence across generations.
frames.concerns: Children as soldiers; Eren's certainty without dharma.

frames.aligns: The cycle of hatred and revenge is the core theme; attachment and fear drive suffering; the ending sides with non-hatred.
frames.concerns: Despair; a suicide attempt; spiked wine (fifth precept).

frames.aligns: Harmony with others restored only through sincerity; ancestors' burdens.
frames.concerns: No sacred framing; impurity of death everywhere.

frames.aligns: Courage to defend the oppressed; anger and ego shown to destroy (Eren); equality of all people against ethnic hatred.
The oneness of humanity: ethnonationalism and collective guilt are condemned, and the ending turns to dialogue across peoples.
frames.concerns: Strong commitment to non-violence; the story offers no spiritual answer.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness: do not murder; seek to live with the truth (Armin, Hange).
Norse myth echoes (Ymir, the world tree) used without mockery; "harm none" ideal set against the cycle of revenge.
Critique of ethnonationalism, propaganda and dehumanization; women soldiers as equals; anti-war ending.
frames.concerns: Critics on the left are split on whether the story undercuts its own anti-fascism; the alt-right fandom and Holocaust-imagery debate; Mikasa's arc centered on Eren; Hange's gender left vague.

frames.aligns: Truth-seeking (Armin, Hange), dialogue across enemy lines, this-life meaning (Armin's "small moments" answer to Zeke).
frames.concerns: Nihilist voices; a suicide attempt (safe-messaging concern).

frames.aligns: Courage, duty, sacrifice for homeland and comrades; loyalty; realism about human evil; respect for soldiers.
frames.concerns: Moral ambiguity; heroes who commit atrocities; authority shown as lying.

frames.aligns: Rebellion against lying authority (the monarchy, the wall cult); pursuit of truth; compassion over tribal hatred.
frames.concerns: Eren's absolute freedom is shown as a trap; harm to children.

frames.aligns: Worth and dignity of the enemy; pluralism and dialogue.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Eren's vow of revenge (ch. 1-2) drives the plot, but the story shows revenge spreading hatred (Gabi kills Sasha, ch. 105) and honors forgiveness (the Blouse family toward Gabi). The ending sides with Armin's dialogue over vengeance (ch. 138-139).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Freedom is the core value: birds and the world beyond the walls; "choose so you won't regret it" (vols. 5-8). Governments that lie are overthrown (Uprising arc, vols. 13-17). Eren's absolute freedom is shown as a trap (ch. 139), which keeps the position below the top.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Loyalty to comrades is honored (Erwin, ch. 80; Hange, ch. 132), but blood loyalty is critiqued: Grisha uses Zeke, Historia defies her father, and ethnic "our people" thinking becomes the Rumbling. Closing hope rests on a cross-national alliance.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: The Survey Corps chain of command (Erwin, Levi) is honored; the walled monarchy and the Church are overthrown (vols. 13-17); Marley's ethnic ranks and armbands are condemned (ch. 86-88).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: The wall cult hides the truth (vol. 9, Uprising arc); the royal pacifism vow is shown as harmful; truth-seeking by Armin and Hange is honored. Faith appears as cult and myth (ch. 122), not as a guide the story endorses.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Security and survival dominate a world that is "cruel"; courage, duty and sacrifice are honored (ch. 80, 132). Curiosity (the ocean, vol. 22) and Armin's "small moments" answer to Zeke (ch. 137 area, likely) give self-expression a place.

folkways.japan: The military chain of command, duty and self-sacrifice for the group echo Japanese norms of group loyalty; producer George Wada linked the walls to the closed nature of Japanese society (Creator context). Critics also read the island-against-the-world story against Japan's wartime history, a reading Isayama has rejected.

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Utilitarianism, Might makes right (critiqued), Collectivism/authoritarianism (critiqued), Expressive individualism (critiqued), Nihilism (critiqued).

entry.heading: Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is lived for others. You protect the weak, honor the dead, keep promises, and pass your will to the next generation. A long or powerful life bought by harming others is worth nothing.

frames.aligns: Evil is shown but never made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7); self-giving love; mercy toward the repentant; honor for parents and the dead.
frames.concerns: Kagaya's self-detonation framed as heroic (CCC 2280-2283); Buddhist and Shinto afterlife imagery, judged by framing.

frames.aligns: Struggle against the passions (Muzan's craving, Kokushibo's envy); repentance at death (Akaza, ch. 156); care for the dead.
frames.concerns: Evil spirits are taken as real in the tradition, so "demons" made sympathetic can blur the line; non-Christian afterlife scenes. Guarding the senses (nepsis) makes the gore itself a concern.

frames.aligns: Clear good and evil; sacrifice for others; honoring parents (Ephesians 6:1).
frames.concerns: Buddhist and Shinto spirituality shown as real (John 14:6); heroic framing of Kagaya's choice. Views vary by congregation because each church is self-governing.

frames.aligns: Redemption themes; Equip.org highlights compassion: "Humanizing is the goal, instead of demonizing," and links it to Romans 2:4. Depicts sin without endorsing it.
frames.concerns: Non-Christian afterlife and spirituality; the story's grace has no source beyond human kindness.

frames.aligns: Clear battle between good and evil; courage and sacrifice.
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": literal demons, spirit encounters with the dead, a fire-god ritual dance honored by the hero's family, all shown in a positive or neutral light. Views range widely between churches.

frames.aligns: Total depravity has an echo: demons are humans whose sin has grown monstrous. Common grace lets families value good art by non-Christians.
frames.concerns: Suicide-adjacent scenes framed as noble (WLC Q136 on self-murder); other religions' afterlife shown as real.

frames.aligns: Two kingdoms: the Corps bears the sword to protect the weak, like lawful authority. Law and gospel: demons cannot save themselves; mercy comes from outside them.
frames.concerns: Non-Christian spirituality. LCMS and WELS families tend to be more cautious than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Holiness of life and works of mercy; prevenient grace has an echo in demons who remember their humanity at the end.
frames.concerns: Suicide-adjacent scenes; some fan service. Holiness churches (Nazarene, Wesleyan) usually more cautious about the content than UMC.

frames.aligns: Just war (Article 37) fits the Corps' fight; good and evil judged by framing, in a strong tradition of fantasy literature (C.S. Lewis).
frames.concerns: Suicide-adjacent scenes framed as heroic. Episcopal and ACNA families differ mainly on gender, not on this content.

frames.aligns: Humility, compassion for enemies, community care.
frames.concerns: Violence shown as heroic is the central concern, and here it is the heroes' main tool throughout (Matthew 5:39). Conservative groups avoid most popular media; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Family as central and eternal; reunion with loved ones after death; service and sacrifice.
frames.concerns: Heroic framing of self-destruction; fan service. Members vary in strictness.

frames.aligns: Self-sacrifice, care for family, clear good and evil.
frames.concerns: The dead are unconscious until the resurrection, so spirits of the dead meeting the living (ch. 66, 156, 163, 200) and a rebirth epilogue conflict with teaching on the state of the dead.

frames.aligns: Love of family, mercy, loyalty.
frames.concerns: Spiritism and spirits of the dead are central motifs (Galatians 5:19-21); fighting as the hero's calling.

frames.aligns: Love and goodness outlast evil; compassion over hatred.
frames.concerns: Evil, death and fear are shown as real and powerful forces, against the teaching that they are not part of God's creation.

frames.aligns: Empathy for the marginalized: demon backstories trace harm to poverty and abuse (ch. 96, 154).
frames.concerns: Traditional gender roles; Nezuko's limited voice; the Rising Sun dispute and Korean historical sensitivities.

frames.aligns: Respect for life and its protection; honoring parents (Exodus 20:12); memory of the dead.
frames.concerns: Self-destruction framed as heroic (suicide traditionally forbidden); a fire-god ritual honored. Tzniut makes the red-light arc and outfits a concern; many Haredi homes restrict such media altogether.

frames.aligns: Respect for life; honoring parents; memory of the dead; tikkun olam echoes in protecting the weak.
frames.concerns: Suicide-adjacent sacrifice framed as heroic, treated with compassion today; modesty values applied by families.

frames.aligns: Protecting the vulnerable; harm traced to poverty and abuse; memory of the dead.
frames.concerns: Suicide-adjacent sacrifice framed as heroic; Korean historical sensitivities (Rising Sun earrings, Kanto massacre reading).

frames.aligns: Family loyalty, care for a sister, patience (sabr), fighting only to stop oppression, forgiveness preferred.
frames.concerns: Polytheistic ritual and afterlife imagery treated as real; self-destruction framed as heroic, read against the prohibition of suicide (Qur'an 4:29).

frames.aligns: Dharma may require righteous fighting (Bhagavad Gita); family duty and respect for elders; karma and rebirth (ch. 205).
frames.concerns: Few message conflicts; some families apply the Gita's tamasic category to the gore.

frames.aligns: Draws on Buddhist ideas: craving (Muzan), compassion for all beings, impermanence, a monk-warrior (Gyomei), rebirth (ch. 205).
frames.concerns: Killing is the plot's solution, against the first precept; demons are destroyed rather than released.

frames.aligns: Kagura dance, sun and purity imagery treated with respect; sincerity (makoto) and gratitude in Tanjiro; oni folklore familiar.
frames.concerns: Little to raise; blood and death are sources of impurity, though shown in a fight against evil.

frames.aligns: Courage to defend the oppressed; the five vices (anger, greed, attachment, ego, lust) shown in villains and condemned; seva-like service of the Corps.
frames.concerns: Little to raise in message; heroic self-destruction may be discussed.

frames.aligns: Service, sacrifice and unity; noble qualities shown as the real strength.
frames.concerns: Strong commitment to non-violence: fighting is the heroes' path throughout.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness precepts: honor parents, help others, do not murder (demons who murder are condemned).
Respect for folk religion, nature and ancestors; "harm none" echoes in protecting the weak; no stereotyping of witches or pagans.
Empathy for the marginalized; harm traced to poverty and abuse; critique of rule by fear.
frames.concerns: Mostly traditional gender roles; Nezuko's silence and adult-form design (Anime Feminist; The Mary Sue); Mitsuri's uniform gag; polygamy played lightly; Korean historical sensitivities; suicide framed as noble.

frames.aligns: Human bonds and the value of a finite life over endless demon life (Kagaya: human thoughts endure, ch. 137); empathy; afterlife scenes read as fiction.
Duty, honor, sacrifice, respect for elders, lineage, protective masculinity. The Federalist praises its "courage, family, strength, and masculine virtue."
frames.concerns: Little in the message; some religious conservatives raise the demonic imagery.

frames.aligns: Compassion and justice (Satanic Temple Tenets 1 and 2); protection of children.
frames.concerns: The story honors self-sacrifice, deference to a revered leader and duty over the self, while self-preservation is the villain's creed, against Church of Satan individualism.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity even of enemies (Tanjiro's mercy); justice for the exploited (Ume, Gyutaro).
frames.concerns: Violence as the main solution; traditional gender roles; Korean historical sensitivities.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Duty and samurai-style service are honored, but personal vendetta is not: Tanjiro mourns the demons he kills, and mercy toward Akaza and Gyutaro (ch. 96, 154-156) is part of the story's ethic. Defending family drives the plot more than defending one's name.

Order vs freedom.evidence: The Demon Slayer Corps has ranks, supply, doctors and discipline (Pragmatic lens). Duty, training and obeying the Corps are celebrated; Muzan's lawless rule by fear is the counter-example (ch. 52).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Family is the central value: a brother guarding his sister, the Corps as a family-like body, Rui's forced "fake family" as its opposite. The epilogue honors descendants and lineage (ch. 205).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Hashira ranks and deference to Kagaya Ubuyashiki are presented with reverence; his servant leadership and self-sacrifice (ch. 137-138) are shown as heroic. Inherited Breathing styles and passing the will down tie worth to lineage and rank.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Buddhist and Shinto motifs are sincere: the blind monk Gyomei, the fire-god kagura dance, spirits of the dead meeting the dying (ch. 66, 156, 163, 179, 200), a rebirth-style epilogue (ch. 205). Doma's cult, not faith itself, is exposed.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Life is lived for others: protect the weak, keep promises, accept early death (the "Mark"). Hard training and self-sacrifice (Rengoku, ch. 66) are the highest goods.

folkways.japan: The Taisho-era setting, Confucian filial piety, samurai ideals of service and death, and Shinto and Buddhist imagery are Japanese traditional values the story treats as true; many readers from other cultures will see these as the setting's norms more than a message aimed at them.

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Confucian ethics, Communitarianism, Dharmic (Buddhist), Traditionalism, Stoicism.

series.title: Tokyo Ghoul
series.native: 東京喰種 トーキョーグール

entry.heading: Tokyo Ghoul
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: Identity is a choice made under pressure: a person who belongs to two worlds can try to protect both, but the story counts the cost of that choice in pain and loss, and offers only a fragile hope that the two sides might one day live together.

content.framing: Neutral; predatory desire shown as menacing

frames.aligns: Dignity of every person, even the "monster"; critique of dehumanizing the outsider; evil (torture, revenge) shown as evil with consequences.
frames.concerns: Despair rather than hope dominates the original ending; revenge is pursued by several sympathetic characters; gratuitous gore in media is criticized by the Church ("Ethics in Communications").

frames.aligns: Struggle with the passions (hunger as a picture of a consuming passion); compassion for the enemy.
frames.concerns: Darkness without theosis or grace; strong concern about images that feed the passions; the church setting used for a cannibal scene (vol. 4-5) touches reverence for holy places.

frames.aligns: Clear depiction of sin's consequences; friendship and sacrifice.
frames.concerns: No saving answer, only human striving; graphic violence and strong language (Ephesians 4:29). Views vary by congregation, since each church is self-governing.

frames.aligns: Beneath the Tangles writers read Kaneki's arc as a search for redemption: "to be human means to feel pain." Evil framed as evil; mercy toward outsiders.
frames.concerns: The redemption remains unfinished; occasional nihilistic voices; gore and language.

frames.aligns: Clear battle between destructive and protective power.
frames.concerns: Ghouls are not demons, but the predatory, possession-like imagery (Rize "inside" Kaneki's mind, ch. 62-63, likely) can concern families attentive to spiritual warfare.

frames.aligns: Total depravity echoed: every faction, human and ghoul, is capable of atrocity; common grace lets families value a serious work by a non-Christian author.
frames.concerns: No providence or grace in view; vengeance taken into human hands (WLC on the sixth commandment).

frames.aligns: Law without gospel: the story shows people unable to save themselves. Two kingdoms: questions about the state's use of force.
frames.concerns: No gospel answer offered; confessional (LCMS, WELS) families more cautious than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Social holiness: concern for the outcast and the hunted; works of mercy (Anteiku feeding ghouls without killing).
frames.concerns: No grace named, and the hope of coexistence is left unfinished. Wesley's rule against diversions that cannot be used "in the name of the Lord Jesus" makes the graphic content a heavy depiction concern for holiness churches (Nazarene, Wesleyan), less for many UMC families.

frames.aligns: Respect for the outsider; just-war questions (Article 37) about the CCG's campaign.
frames.concerns: Despair at the end; revenge cycles. Episcopal and ACNA families differ more on gender than on this content.

frames.aligns: The cycle of violence is shown as destroying everyone; Anteiku's nonviolent ethic and Kaneki's mother's "better to be hurt" echo nonresistance.
frames.concerns: Kaneki abandons that ethic and the story makes his violence effective. Conservative groups avoid such media entirely; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Agency and the struggle of a divided nature; family love; service.
frames.concerns: A bleak ending with no hope beyond human effort; revenge pursued by sympathetic characters. For the Strength of Youth asks for media that invites the Spirit; the gore and language are the depiction issue. Members vary in strictness.

frames.aligns: Concern for the outcast; consequences of evil; the body treated as something that matters.
frames.concerns: Adventist teaching on media (drawn from Ellen G. White and the church's guidelines) warns against entertainment that dwells on violence and horror; the cannibal premise also clashes with the health message. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Prejudice shown as wrong; peace preferred to violence.
frames.concerns: Witness publications (Watchtower, jw.org guidance on entertainment) counsel avoiding media that features violence (Psalm 11:5); fighting is the main way the story's conflicts are settled, though it is framed as tragedy, and the horror imagery is a heavy depiction concern. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Compassion and the hope of reconciliation.
frames.concerns: Christian Science teaching stresses spiritual reality over material sense, so media that dwells on bodily horror, disease and death runs against the habit of thought it encourages. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Strong critique of prejudice and state violence against a minority; empathy for the marginalized; Ishida's majority/minority framing.
frames.concerns: Glorified fighting in places; little agency for some female characters; mental-health portrayal needs care.

frames.aligns: Respect for life; warning against dehumanizing a people; memory of the dead; revenge shown as a cycle that destroys (Leviticus 19:18).
frames.concerns: Eating human flesh and blood breaks food and purity law in its deepest form, though the story frames it as horror. Lashon hara and nivul peh make the language a concern; many Haredi homes avoid such media entirely.

frames.aligns: Respect for life; warning against dehumanizing a people; revenge rejected by the story's outcome.
frames.concerns: No turn toward repair at the end. Degrading content and vulgar speech are weighed by values of dignity; the cannibal premise is jarring for families who keep kosher.

frames.aligns: A plea against dehumanizing a minority, close to the prophetic call to justice; empathy for the hunted; cruelty shown as cruelty.
frames.concerns: Glorified fighting in places; few women with full arcs. Cruelty and exploitation are the ethical tests for the explicitness.

frames.aligns: Justice for the oppressed; mercy; patience under suffering (sabr).
frames.concerns: Revenge pursued by sympathetic characters; no turn to God or mercy beyond human effort; the premise breaks the deepest taboo, eating human flesh, which the Qur'an (49:12) uses as the image of backbiting, though the story frames it as horror. Foul language and graphic violence are a heavy depiction concern.

frames.aligns: Dharma under impossible duties; karma of violence returning on all sides.
frames.concerns: Ahimsa and vegetarian traditions find the premise especially repellent; despair at the end.

frames.aligns: Craving (hunger) as the root of suffering; compassion for all beings; cycles of harm.
frames.concerns: First precept: killing is central; no liberation shown.

frames.aligns: Harmony and the hope of coexistence.
frames.concerns: Blood, death and corpses are kegare (impurity), so a story built on them weighs as depiction; no shrines or kami are mocked, which is this tradition's main concern. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Equality of all people; standing against injustice (the sant-sipahi ideal); service.
frames.concerns: Violence for revenge rather than defense of the oppressed; Sikh codes forbid intoxicants and many Sikhs avoid meat, so the premise is jarring. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: The oneness of humanity and coexistence of opposed groups is the series' hope.
frames.concerns: Bahá'í writings counsel avoiding backbiting and degrading influences; heavy violence. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Individual spiritual identity surviving trauma.
frames.concerns: Scientology opposes psychiatry and psychiatric drugs; Kanou's surgical experiments and the CCG's medicalized control are framed as horrors, which fits concerns it raises, though the series' trauma framing differs. "Do not murder" (The Way to Happiness) and glorified violence in places. No public Scientology guidance on manga found. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Respect for nature and for beings unlike us; balance.
frames.concerns: The Wiccan Rede "an it harm none" is broken by every faction; revenge. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Critique of prejudice against a minority and of state violence; empathy for the hunted; Ishida's majority/minority statement.
frames.concerns: Few women with full arcs; Tsukiyama's coding mixes queer and predatory traits; safe-messaging concerns about self-harm and suicidal thinking.

frames.aligns: Reason, empathy and the value of a finite human life; refusal of easy good and evil.
frames.concerns: Glorified fighting; mental-health portrayal without support or recovery; bleak ending.

frames.aligns: Loyalty, protecting friends, a café that keeps order and restraint.
frames.concerns: Anti-authority strand (the CCG as oppressor); violence, language and moral grayness; no clear heroes.

frames.aligns: The Satanic Temple's tenets of compassion and justice, and the Church of Satan's focus on the individual, fit the story's sympathy for the outcast and its critique of the herd. (from general knowledge; to verify)
frames.concerns: Cruelty and non-consensual harm conflict with TST's tenets on bodily autonomy.

frames.aligns: First Principle, the inherent worth and dignity of every person, extended to the "other"; justice and compassion.
frames.concerns: Violence and despair; no community repair at the end. (from general knowledge; to verify)

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Revenge spreads harm: Mado's zeal and Touka's attacks (ch. 13-29) and Yamori repeating his own abuse (ch. 59-66). Kaneki's hardening to protect friends brings him no peace (ch. 80-94).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Authority on both sides, the CCG and Aogiri, uses violence as policy and is critiqued. Anteiku's quiet restraint, outside both systems, is the endorsed path.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Found family and protecting one's group come first (Anteiku, the Kirishima siblings, Hinami). Hide's friendship regardless of what Kaneki is, and the hope of coexistence, widen the circle.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: A hidden minority hunted by an organized majority; prejudice and state violence are critiqued. Aogiri's "strong eat the weak" creed is shown as hollow.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Christian imagery recurs ("Original Sin," ch. 126; the church fight, vol. 4-5) but is symbolic and offers no rescue. Kanou's lab science is shown as horror (ch. 95-111), so neither pole is celebrated.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Survival dominates a world of constant death, but the story's central value is tolerance across groups and the choice of one's own identity (life message).

folkways.japan: Ishida's sense of being "between the majority and minority groups" speaks to conformity pressure in Japanese society; Kaneki's mother's ethic, "better to be hurt than to hurt others," echoes Japanese ideals of self-effacement that the story tests and then breaks.

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Critical theory, Might makes right (critiqued), Communitarianism, Nihilism (explored).

entry.heading: Goodnight Punpun
entry.label: From summaries

frames.aligns: Takes suffering, guilt and the need for repentance seriously; the mother's deathbed apology; the dignity of a wounded person who keeps living; sin is never made attractive (Inter Mirifica 7).
frames.concerns: Asano's relativism; no hope beyond human ties; a planned abortion left unjudged (CCC 2270-2275); a comic "God." Sex outside marriage, sexual abuse and repeated suicide on the page are a heavy depiction concern (CCC 2280-2283, 2521-2524).

frames.aligns: Close to a study of the passions (despair, lust, self-love) and of a soul without spiritual guidance; their cost is never hidden.
frames.concerns: Despair is left without any answer of grace or repentance in the tradition's terms; a comic "God" figure. Watchfulness over the senses (nepsis) makes the sexual imagery and suicide scenes a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Honest about the emptiness of a life without hope; sin's consequences are not hidden.
frames.concerns: No hope in Christ or anything beyond survival; relativism; the abortion storyline. Under Philippians 4:8, the sexual content, abuse, profanity and suicide are a heavy depiction concern. Each congregation is self-governing, so views vary.

frames.aligns: A realistic picture of a fallen world and broken homes; the need for rescue that no human romance can supply. Many in this tradition distinguish depicting sin from endorsing it.
frames.concerns: No gospel answer; relativism; the abortion plan. Explicitness is high even for families who "engage" culture.

frames.aligns: No occult or demonic content; a vivid picture of spiritual emptiness; cults shown as deadly.
frames.concerns: No spiritual answer; a comic "God" summoned by a chant; spiritual deception (the Pegasus group) shown ambiguously. Holiness standards make the sexual content a heavy depiction concern.

frames.aligns: Total depravity has a strong echo: no character is innocent, including the protagonist. Common grace lets adults value serious art by non-Christians.
frames.concerns: Sin without grace; relativism; abortion. WLC Q139 makes the sexual imagery a heavy depiction concern; suicide as self-murder (WLC Q136), treated pastorally.

frames.aligns: Law without gospel: a person crushed by guilt with no word of forgiveness, shown honestly.
frames.concerns: No gospel offered. Entertainment is judged by conscience; LCMS and WELS families are typically more cautious than ELCA about the explicitness.

frames.aligns: Prevenient grace has an echo in the friends who keep reaching for Punpun (Sachi); social holiness in who failed these children.
frames.concerns: No grace named; abortion. Holiness churches (Nazarene, Wesleyan) are far more cautious than UMC about the sexual content and suicide scenes.

frames.aligns: Moral seriousness about suffering and guilt in the line of serious literary fiction; pastoral approach to suicide; works judged by how they frame good and evil.
frames.concerns: Relativism; abortion; no answer of grace. Episcopal and ACNA families may differ on how much adult literary content they allow.

frames.aligns: Community care as the missing thing; the killing leads only to ruin; no violence shown as heroic.
frames.concerns: A world with no church or community to catch anyone, and no answer beyond private survival. Separation from worldly media makes the explicitness a heavy concern; Old Order groups would avoid it, MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Family as the thing that matters most, shown by its absence; repentance and forgiveness (the mother).
frames.concerns: No plan of salvation or hope beyond survival; relativism; abortion. For the Strength of Youth asks for media that invites the Spirit; the sexual content, profanity and suicide put it outside youth guidance.

frames.aligns: The cost of broken homes and unhealthy lives is shown, not admired.
frames.concerns: No hope beyond survival; abortion; a comic "God." Fundamental Belief 22 and "by beholding we become changed" make the sexual content and despair a heavy depiction concern.

frames.aligns: Immorality and violence are shown as harmful, not admired; cults shown as deadly.
frames.concerns: No hope in God's Kingdom; relativism; abortion. jw.org counsel on entertainment that features immorality and violence makes the explicitness a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Love and friendship (Sachi) are what save Punpun's life.
frames.concerns: Despair, sickness and death are presented as the final reality, against the teaching that they have no place in God's creation. Members guard thought ("Stand porter at the door of thought," Science and Health 392), so dwelling on these depictions is a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Honest treatment of mental illness, abuse and family violence; a male abuse survivor taken seriously; compassion for the broken.
frames.concerns: Women often written as damaged or rescuers; the protagonist's coercion little addressed. Suicide scenes against safe-messaging norms are a depiction concern, Significant for younger readers.

frames.aligns: Respect for this life; the duty to preserve life (pikuach nefesh) underlined by its loss; teshuvah in the mother's apology.
frames.concerns: Relativism; abortion views differ from the story's silence; a comic "God." Tzniut and nivul peh make the sexual content and language a heavy concern; many Haredi homes avoid such media entirely.

frames.aligns: Choosing life; teshuvah; the dignity of the wounded.
frames.concerns: Relativism; the abortion storyline is not weighed. Degrading sexual content and vulgar speech are a concern under Jewish values of modesty and dignity.

frames.aligns: Honest about abuse, cruelty and exploitation as harm; compassion for the broken.
frames.concerns: Women as damaged rescuers; the protagonist's coercion. Suicide content is a depiction concern, Significant for younger readers.

frames.aligns: Patience (sabr) and endurance; family obligations shown by their breakdown.
frames.concerns: Despair of God's mercy is warned against (Qur'an 39:53), and the story offers no mercy beyond survival; a man's face drawn and called "God" touches the rule against depicting God; abortion. Lowering the gaze (Qur'an 24:30-31) makes the sexual content and nudity a heavy concern.

frames.aligns: Karma-like chains of cause and effect across a family; the duty of parents (dharma) shown by its failure.
frames.concerns: No path of release offered; suicide discouraged. Tamasic content under Gita 17 is a depiction matter; views vary by community.

frames.aligns: Close to Buddhist teaching on suffering, craving and clinging: Punpun's attachment to Aiko and to an idealized self drives the tragedy; impermanence and an open ending.
frames.concerns: No path beyond suffering is shown. Right mindfulness of what feeds the mind makes the sexual and suicide scenes a depiction concern, Significant for younger readers.

frames.aligns: Sincerity and its absence; ordinary life and community repair after impurity and loss.
frames.concerns: No doctrine on fiction; no shrines or kami are mocked. Death and blood as kegare may weigh with some families.

frames.aligns: The five vices (lust, anger, greed, attachment, ego) shown as destructive, not admirable; attachment to Aiko as the root of ruin; seva in Sachi's friendship.
frames.concerns: No spiritual answer. Lust shown on the page is a depiction concern.

frames.aligns: Sexual harm and family breakdown shown as damaging; friendship as service.
frames.concerns: No spiritual answer; relativism. Shoghi Effendi's call to a "chaste and holy life" makes the sexual content a heavy depiction concern.

frames.aligns: Survival as the core urge across the dynamics (self, family, groups); a person who keeps living; cults that harm members shown as harmful.
frames.concerns: Depression framed through trauma; any push toward psychiatric help would run against the church's stance. No content code for fiction.

frames.aligns: Personal responsibility; harm shown as harm (the Rede); no stereotyped witches or pagans.
frames.concerns: Little hope offered. The Rede ("harm none") underlines the abuse and killing.

frames.aligns: Serious treatment of depression, family violence and a male abuse survivor; no glamorized fan service; critique of cult control.
frames.concerns: Women written as damaged rescuers; the protagonist's sexual coercion little addressed. Suicide shown repeatedly, possibly including a hanging, which safe-messaging guidelines advise against.

frames.aligns: This-life focus; human connection and ordinary work as what keeps a person going; critique of cults and magical thinking.
frames.concerns: Little model of recovery. Cruelty and the suicide scenes are a depiction concern, Significant for minors.

frames.aligns: Shows the cost of broken families and absent fathers; no glamour in the sex or violence; responsibility shown by its failure.
frames.concerns: Relativism; abortion; a protagonist who abandons his responsibilities. Content that degrades the good, the true and the beautiful is a depiction concern.

frames.aligns: Life lived now, with no afterlife; critique of cults and of messianic hope; harm to a minor and unwanted sexual advances, which the Eleven Rules condemn, framed as harm.
frames.concerns: Little self-determination shown; Punpun is mostly passive. Harm to children shown on the page is the depiction concern.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity of the wounded; compassion; honest search for meaning without a given answer.
frames.concerns: Women as damaged rescuers; little community repair. Age-appropriateness makes it adult reading.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: No act of revenge or defense of honor is celebrated: Punpun's killing of Mitsuko (ch. ~113-114) leads only to flight and loss, and Asano says he does not think Punpun is a "good person."

Order vs freedom.evidence: No institution rescues anyone, and Asano's frame is pluralist: "the world has many different values, but none of them are 'right.'" The story neither celebrates rules nor romanticizes freedom; the Kagoshima escape fails.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Families are broken (father's assault, Aiko's cult stepmother, Midori's abuse, ch. 50). What helps is a friend who intervenes (Sachi stops Punpun's suicide attempt) and a mother's late apology.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Adult power over children is the main form of power, and it is shown as harmful (Socio-cultural lens). No leader or elder is held up for deference.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Religion appears as a comic inner "God" voice and as cults that fail to save (Aiko's stepmother; Pegasus's group). The ending rests on ordinary secular survival: a job, time, a few ties.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: The ending values plain survival and work, but Sachi's creative ambition and the story's tolerance for many values pull toward self-expression.

folkways.japan: The pressure to appear normal, social withdrawal, silence about family violence and the I-novel tradition of confession are Japanese context the essay notes; the story criticizes these more than it endorses them.

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Nihilism (explored, not affirmed), Absurdism, Dharmic (Buddhist) by echo, Postmodernism.

series.title: My Hero Academia
series.native: 僕のヒーローアカデミア

entry.heading: My Hero Academia (Boku no Hero Academia)
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A good life is spent helping others without being asked, even at cost to yourself; and real heroism means reaching out to save the person no one else will, including the "villain".

content.framing: Mixed: Mineta's behavior is mostly condemned or punished by classmates; adult heroine costumes are neutral

frames.aligns: Self-giving love and mercy toward enemies fit the call to love enemies; Endeavor's and Bakugo's repentance mirror conversion; dignity of the weak (a Quirkless boy). Evil is not made attractive.
frames.concerns: Mineta's harassment as comedy; vestiges as quasi-spirits, judged by framing (CCC 2115-2117); trans-coded characters for some families.

frames.aligns: Growth through humility and struggle; repentance (metanoia) taken seriously; respect for elders and teachers.
frames.concerns: Spirit-like vestiges and a demon-like villain; combat as the main path of heroism (St. Basil's canon calls even justified killing a matter for repentance). Fan service as stirring the passions.

frames.aligns: Clear good and evil at the end; repentance and personal responsibility (Bakugo's apology); protecting the weak.
frames.concerns: Peeping gags played for laughs; trans-coded characters (BF&M 2000 Art. XVIII); occult-flavored vestiges. Views vary by congregation, since each church is self-governing.

frames.aligns: "No one is too far gone" redemption (Beneath the Tangles); servant heroism; "anyone can be a hero who stands up for justice" (Plugged In).
frames.concerns: Sympathetic villains need discussion; harassment gags.

frames.aligns: Courage, self-sacrifice, deliverance of the oppressed (Eri).
frames.concerns: Media as an "open door": vestige spirits living in a body, a power passed by consuming hair, a demon-like immortal villain.

frames.aligns: Common grace: real goods (courage, mercy) in a non-Christian story; everyone, heroes included, carries guilt.
frames.concerns: The story locates evil partly in society rather than the heart, which critics on both left and right dispute. Fan service (WLC Q139).

frames.aligns: Two kingdoms: licensed heroes as a civil vocation that restrains evil; law and gospel: Bakugo and Endeavor face the law of their guilt, then receive undeserved forgiveness.
frames.concerns: Harassment gags; LCMS and ELCA families may differ on the trans-coded characters.

frames.aligns: Prevenient grace: the story insists even Shigaraki can be reached; social holiness: care for abused children and outsiders.
frames.concerns: Fan service against holiness standards. UMC (affirming) and holiness bodies may read the LGBTQ elements differently.

frames.aligns: Just-war framing (Article 37) fits defensive hero work; reconciliation of the Todoroki family; works judged by how they frame good and evil.
frames.concerns: Episcopal and ACNA families may differ on LGBTQ elements.

frames.aligns: Enemy love: Deku's goal in the climax is to save Shigaraki, not destroy him; mutual aid in the finale (friends build Deku's suit).
frames.concerns: Violence shown as heroic is the central concern, and combat is the main form of heroism throughout (Matthew 5:39); a fame-driven "world." Conservative groups would likely avoid it; MC USA families may read it with discussion.

frames.aligns: Family repair, honoring mothers, hard work and service; chaste romance; agency.
frames.concerns: Vestige spirits for some; harassment gags.

frames.aligns: Service, self-sacrifice, repentance; care for abused children.
frames.concerns: Vestiges of the dead speaking inside Deku conflict with teaching that the dead are unconscious; combat as heroism.

frames.aligns: Love of neighbor, honesty, repentance.
frames.concerns: Fighting as the noblest calling and celebrated hero combat (Psalm 11:5); spirits of the dead living on (vestiges); trans-coded characters.

frames.aligns: Overcoming limitation; love as the answer to hate; healing of relationships.
frames.concerns: Evil and suffering treated as powerful realities; fear-based villains.

frames.aligns: Social justice: neglected children, a corrupt state Commission, outsiders; reform at the end.
frames.concerns: Mineta's harassment played for laughs; Anime Feminist's critique of how Magne is treated.

frames.aligns: Pikuach nefesh: saving life is the hero's job; teshuvah in Bakugo and Endeavor; honoring parents with limits on abuse.
frames.concerns: Lashon hara in Bakugo's insults; trans-coded characters. Tzniut makes the costumes and gags a concern; many Haredi homes avoid such media.

frames.aligns: Saving life, teshuvah, honoring parents with limits on abuse; kind speech valued against Bakugo's insults.
frames.concerns: The 2020 "Maruta" name echoed a WWII atrocity, which some families may want to discuss.

frames.aligns: Tikkun olam: reform of an unjust system; dignity of outsiders and trans characters (Tiger).
frames.concerns: The "Maruta" name controversy; Magne's treatment (Anime Feminist).

frames.aligns: Courage, protecting the weak, justice against corrupt authority, respect for mothers, mercy to wrongdoers who repent.
frames.concerns: Vestige spirits for some; harassment gags; trans-coded characters. Haya (modesty) makes the costumes a concern.

frames.aligns: Dharma: duty and righteous fighting to protect others (Gita); respect for teachers and elders (guru-shishya echo in All Might and Deku).
Suffering caused by craving for status (Endeavor) and hatred (Shigaraki); compassion for the enemy's suffering "inner child"; impermanence of power (Deku loses One For All).
frames.concerns: First precept (non-harm): violence is the main solution; harsh speech.

frames.aligns: Respect for ancestors (vestiges as forebears who guide); sincerity and gratitude; harmony restored to the community.
Courage to defend the oppressed; seva (selfless service); ego (haumai) and anger in Endeavor and Bakugo shown as faults to overcome.
Service, unity, the oneness of humanity (no one is beyond reach).
frames.concerns: Combat as the main form of service, against a strong commitment to non-violence; harassment gags.

frames.aligns: The Way to Happiness: help others, set a good example, honor parents (with abuse condemned).
frames.concerns: Mental illness shown mostly in villains (Anime Feminist), a theme the Church reads through its own critique of psychiatry.

frames.aligns: Personal responsibility; "harm none" in saving rather than destroying; inclusion.
Critique of a celebrity, profit-driven system; attention to abused children and outsiders; social reform at the end.
frames.concerns: Mineta's harassment played for laughs; Anime Feminist argues the series is "conservative": Magne killed and misgendered, mental illness mostly shown in villains, heroes as a "Thin Blue Line"; others read the late arcs as systemic critique.

frames.aligns: Reason, training and human solidarity; Horikoshi: "anyone can be a hero" (VIZ, 2024); no supernatural reward.
Duty, discipline, mentorship, merit, family repair, institutions reformed rather than torn down; clear good and evil at the end.
frames.concerns: Sympathy for villains may blur moral lines; LGBTQ characters for some families; anti-authority arcs (the Commission).

frames.aligns: Challenges corrupt authority (the Commission); compassion and justice (Satanic Temple Tenets 1 and 2); "anyone can be a hero."
frames.concerns: Institutions reformed rather than challenged; self-sacrifice over self-preservation.

frames.aligns: Inherent worth and dignity of everyone, even the villain; justice for neglected children.
frames.concerns: Magne's treatment and misgendering (Anime Feminist); harassment gags.

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Heroism means reaching out to save even the villain (Deku and Shigaraki); Stain's purity killings are condemned. Bakugo's pride ends in apology (ch. 323), and forgiveness is honored over vengeance.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Training, teamwork and school discipline win, and reckless solo heroics are punished. The Hero Commission's secret killings are exposed (ch. 314), and the story chooses reform from within.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Help everyone, without being asked. Endeavor's breeding of children for power is condemned (ch. 39, 290-291); found family in Class 1-A carries the warmth (ch. 319-323).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Hero rankings and the single "Symbol of Peace" are critiqued; "anyone can be a hero" (Horikoshi, 2024). Mentorship and passing power down (All Might to Deku) are honored.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: No real-world faith shapes the plot; vestiges of past users live on inside One For All. Readers find redemption themes, but institutions, science and reform drive the plot.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Helping others and peace are the aims; Toga's self-expression is treated with sympathy and caution (ch. 391-395). War and mass casualties in later volumes keep security in view.

folkways.japan: The school-club and sports-festival culture, respect for teachers and the shonen ideal of friendship, effort and victory are Japanese school norms the story uses as its setting, while its critique of hero celebrity and a state commission is its own message.

entry.dominant: Classical virtue ethics, Communitarianism, Might makes right (critiqued), Christian (redemptive) themes, Critical theory (contested), Traditionalism.

entry.heading: One-Punch Man
entry.label: From summaries
entry.life_message: A hero is someone who keeps helping people and keeps fighting, without needing praise, rank or even a challenge. Strength, fame and status are empty if they are the goal. Doing the right thing for its own sake is what counts.

content.framing: Neutral (comic) to Shown with consequences (late arcs)
Neutral (played for gags and pin-up appeal)

frames.aligns: Humility; doing good without seeking glory; mercy toward a defeated enemy (Garou is spared); pride and vanity in the Hero Association shown as empty.
frames.concerns: Fan service is offered for enjoyment, not framed as a problem (CCC 2521-2524 on modesty); same-sex attraction treated as comedy (CCC 2357-2359 asks respect for persons). Gore is a depiction matter.

frames.aligns: Hidden, humble virtue against vainglory (heroes who chase rank); the false "God" who buys loyalty with power is framed as evil.
frames.concerns: Saitama's listlessness is never named as a spiritual struggle; sexual imagery stirs the "passions." Some priests and parishes weigh the imagery more heavily.

frames.aligns: Clear good and evil; hard work; doing good unseen (Matthew 6:1-4).
frames.concerns: Fan service and a same-sex gag character presented without critique; mild profanity (Ephesians 4:29). Views vary by congregation because each church is self-governing.

frames.aligns: Christ and Pop Culture reads the series as saying "A hero is not simply one who wins; a hero is one who fights," and links it to faithful effort, with the outcome left to God.
frames.concerns: Fan service presented approvingly; Puri-Puri Prisoner; a world with no real God.

frames.aligns: Courage against overwhelming evil; the being called "God," who grants power for loyalty, is clearly framed as a threat.
frames.concerns: A supernatural power-giver and a seer's prophecy may still raise spiritual-warfare caution for some families; fan service and modesty. Views range widely between churches.

frames.aligns: Common grace lets families value well-made satire by non-Christians; the critique of human pride and fame-seeking fits a doctrine of human sinfulness.
frames.concerns: Fan service (WLC Q139) and the same-sex gag presented without critique.

frames.aligns: Two kingdoms: heroes as an imperfect civil order that still restrains evil. Vocation in ordinary work.
frames.concerns: Fan service; the public's slander of Saitama goes uncorrected. LCMS and WELS families tend to be more cautious than ELCA families.

frames.aligns: Doing good without reward; care for the weak; mercy to Garou.
frames.concerns: Fan service presented approvingly. Holiness churches (Nazarene, Wesleyan) usually more cautious than UMC.

frames.aligns: Just defense against evil; humility; satire of pride, which has a long Anglican literary tradition.
frames.concerns: Fan service. Episcopal and ACNA families differ mainly on the Puri-Puri Prisoner question.

frames.aligns: Humility, refusal of status and rank, service without reward, sparing Garou.
frames.concerns: Violence is the story's normal and celebrated way to solve problems (Matthew 5:39), a message issue, not only a depiction one; worldly fame is mocked but the world's methods are kept. Conservative groups avoid much of this media; MC USA families vary.

frames.aligns: Hard work, self-discipline, service, honesty about one's limits.
frames.concerns: For the Strength of Youth warns against media that is "vulgar, immoral, violent"; the fan service is presented for enjoyment. Members vary in strictness.

frames.aligns: Discipline, healthy routine (Saitama's daily training), humble service, honesty.
frames.concerns: Adventist counsel on media ("by beholding we become changed", from Ellen G. White's writings) asks members to avoid entertainment that makes violence enjoyable; here fighting is the fun of the story, a message issue as well as a depiction one. Fan service; seer's prophecy. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Humility, honesty, not seeking prominence.
frames.concerns: Watchtower publications counsel avoiding entertainment that features violence, spiritism or immorality; violence presented as entertainment, a supernatural power-giver and a seer's prophecy, fan service and a same-sex gag character all fall under that counsel. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Goodness shown as stronger than evil; quiet service; emptiness of material power and status.
frames.concerns: Focus on matter and bodily force; the tradition's emphasis on filling thought with what is good (Mary Baker Eddy's writings) makes fan service and gore a concern. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Satire of status and celebrity; sympathy for the overlooked (Garou's argument about who gets cast as the monster).
frames.concerns: Women drawn for fan service; Puri-Puri Prisoner as a possible stereotype; violence as entertainment.

frames.aligns: Humility; protecting life; doing good without seeking reward, close to the highest levels of tzedakah.
frames.concerns: Fan service presented approvingly; a same-sex gag character. Tzniut makes the fan service a heavy depiction concern; many Haredi homes restrict secular media like this entirely, while Modern Orthodox families are selective.

frames.aligns: Humility; protecting life; doing good without seeking reward.
frames.concerns: Fan service presented approvingly; the same-sex gag weighs differently by family. Modesty and dignity are the values families apply to the fan service.

frames.aligns: Humility; service to others without reward as a form of tikkun olam; satire of status and fame.
frames.concerns: Puri-Puri Prisoner as a possible stereotype; women drawn for fan service. Stereotypes and exploitation are the ethical tests, not ritual law.

frames.aligns: Humility; patience; protecting the weak; sincerity of intention (doing good not for show); the false "God" is framed as evil.
frames.concerns: Fan service presented approvingly against haya; a same-sex gag character; the word "God" used for a malevolent being may be uncomfortable for some families.

frames.aligns: Nishkama karma: Saitama acts without attachment to reward (Bhagavad Gita 2:47); righteous fighting against evil; respect between master and disciple.
frames.concerns: Some modesty concerns; little else at the level of message.

frames.aligns: Emptiness of fame and status; suffering from craving (heroes chasing rank, Garou chasing strength); Saitama's calm.
frames.concerns: Killing is treated as normal and fun (first precept); fan service (third precept).

frames.aligns: Sincerity (makoto), humility, protecting the community, order restored after disaster.
frames.concerns: Little at the level of message. The malevolent "God" is not a kami in the Shinto sense; some may find the word use odd. Gore relates to ideas of impurity (kegare) only loosely. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Seva (selfless service), nimrata (humility), the saint-soldier ideal of fighting only to protect the weak, and critique of haumai (ego) in the status-hungry heroes. (from general knowledge; to verify)
frames.concerns: Lust (kaam) is one of the five thieves, so the fan service is a concern; violence played for comedy sits uneasily with fighting only for justice. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Service to humanity, humility, unity across differences, a sympathetic hearing for the outsider (Garou).
frames.concerns: Bahá'í teaching values chastity and moderation and turns away from conflict as a solution; fighting is the story's main tool and fan service is presented approvingly. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Competence, self-improvement through training, helping others, and "Safeguard and improve your environment" and "Do not harm a person of good will" from The Way to Happiness.
frames.concerns: Saitama's emptiness is never addressed; harm to bystanders is treated lightly. The church's own published materials say little about anime. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Personal responsibility, self-made meaning; the false "God" demanding loyalty is framed as evil.
frames.concerns: The one nature-worshipping figure, Vaccine Man, is a villain who calls himself Mother Earth's apostle, so reverence for the Earth is played as monstrous; the Wiccan Rede ("harm none") contrasts with violence as fun. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Satire of status, celebrity and institutions; sympathy for outsiders; a powerful female psychic.
frames.concerns: At the message level, fan service (including a young-looking adult woman, Tatsumaki) is presented for the viewer's enjoyment, and the gay character is partly a joke.

frames.aligns: Meaning made by one's own choices; skepticism of institutions and prophecy; the only "god" is a manipulator; mercy and reason.
frames.concerns: Saitama's emptiness is left unresolved and may need a mental-health conversation.

frames.aligns: Hard work, self-reliance, humility, protecting the public; satire of bureaucracy; mentor and disciple.
frames.concerns: Fan service; Puri-Puri Prisoner; little family life.

frames.aligns: Non-theistic Satanists (Church of Satan; The Satanic Temple) value self-reliance, skepticism of imposed authority and earned strength; Saitama is a self-made individual outside institutions, and the story's only "God" is a manipulator who buys loyalty. TST's tenets on compassion and justice fit Saitama's mercy. (from general knowledge; to verify)
frames.concerns: Little at the level of message; The Satanic Temple's tenet on bodily autonomy and respect for others may make the gay gag a minor point. (from general knowledge; to verify)

frames.aligns: Inherent worth of every person, including outsiders like Garou; compassion; satire of status and unfair systems.
frames.concerns: Women drawn for fan service; Puri-Puri Prisoner as a joke at a gay man's expense; violence as entertainment. (from general knowledge; to verify)

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Saitama gives up credit and takes the blame in the rain (Deep Sea King arc, ch. 21-29); doing good without praise is the life message. Genos's revenge is softened by loyalty.

Order vs freedom.evidence: Institutions are mocked but not abolished: the Hero Association is bureaucratic and image-driven yet organizes defense (Pragmatic lens). Saitama does good on his own terms.

Civic vs kin.evidence: Heroes help whoever is in danger; family barely appears. The outsider Garou's grievance against a system that needs villains is taken seriously (Garou arc).

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: The ranking system is the main satire: status-seeking heroes are exposed in crises, and the weakest C-class hero, Mumen Rider, is honored for courage (ch. 26-28).

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Mostly secular; a being called "God" who grants power for loyalty is a cosmic threat (Online Punch 162-168). Training routine and ordinary effort explain strength.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Meaning comes from small, ordinary goods: groceries on sale, meals with friends (Philosophy essay). Saitama's boredom after winning is an existential, self-expression question rather than a survival one.

folkways.japan: Rankings, sponsorship and the salaryman background (Saitama as a failed job-seeker) satirize Japanese corporate and celebrity culture; the humility of doing good without credit echoes Japanese ideals of modesty as much as the story's own message.

entry.dominant: Existentialism, Classical virtue ethics, Absurdism, Might makes right (critiqued), Stoicism.
